work.author: Origen
work.title: Homiliae in Job (fragmenta in catenis, typus II)

paragraphs.text: Origen's Exegetical Notes on Job
Chapter 1

Verse 10. "Have you not fenced in what is outside him?" How do you know that he has been fenced in? This adversary of ours, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. So he came around Job too, wanting to do the same things to him. Later, once he had received authority, he did them. And he realized that everything had been fenced in because he had been prevented. Wanting to act against Job, he said: "You have fenced in what is inside him and what is outside him." So you have fenced in everything that has not been handed over to the devil.
Verse 18. While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said to Job: "While your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking at the house of their elder brother,
Verse 19. suddenly a great wind came from the desert and struck the four corners of the house, and the house fell on your children, and they died. I alone escaped, and I have come to tell you."

He made the camels fall to the horsemen, and the donkeys and the yokes of oxen to the raiders. But he hated the sheep, and that is why he brought fire down on them. He plotted against the sons as well, and looked for an opportunity to destroy them. If he had found them reading, he would not have touched the house, and he would have had no chance to kill them. If he had found them praying, he could have done nothing against them. But when he found the right moment, he prevailed. What was the moment? There was drunkenness; there was a banquet. As for the wind striking the corners of the house, note that the hypocrites stand and pray on the corners of the broad streets. Everyone who has not set foot on the straight way makes use of corners, and the broad corner is wickedness that is great and unrestrained.
Chapter 2
Verse 2. And the Lord said to the devil: "Where have you come from?"
God saw how Satan was ashamed and in distress. But when he questions someone and sees him being obstinate, he convicts him of his wrongdoing, as he convicted Cain.
Verse 9. After much time had passed, his wife said to him:

See the villainy. He attacks only when much time has gone by, because that is when a person's strength is weakest. The weakness was twofold: the sufferer had grown weaker over the length of time, and his hope had been given up still more. And a little later: Let us not, then, look at the fact that she is a woman, but at what she advises. I urge people today to do the same: do not look at the rank of the persons, but at the kind of advice they give. A wife exists to help, not to trip up.

Verse 9. His wife said to him: "How long will you endure?" Last of all the devil brings forward the strongest of all the devices he had used before. If only you had taken her too! If only you had buried her with the children! Some say that the words were not even the wife's, but that he took on her form and uttered them himself, since Job's wife could not have been such a woman, unless one were to say that calamity overturned her and made her so. And a little later: Probably this was not the first time she gave this advice; he had often heard many harsher things than these from his wife. See the devil's deceit. He remembered Eve. "This," he says, "brought down the first man; this will be able to overcome this man too." But, wretched and foolish one! She found that man weaker than his belly and sowed her poison in him. This man, however, you see living as a philosopher and rising above nature itself. The loss of his wealth did not bend him, nor the untimely death of his children, nor torment of body with no relief, nor so great a length of time. And do you expect to subdue with words the man whom events could not capture? By the same author.
Why do you weaken the athlete? Why do you hold back his hands? You ought to have said, with the Apostle: "Yet a little while, yet a little while."
Verse 9. "But speak some word against the Lord, and die."

Only after recounting the tragedy in detail does she bring in her shameless advice. Even then she did not say to him openly, "Blaspheme." For people who give wicked advice do not dare to present it uncovered. What are you saying, woman? You ought to appease him, you ought to reconcile him, and do you instead urge provoking him? For if God did these things, one must entreat him, not blaspheme him. And how is it clear that I shall die even if I do speak [?]? But see what the woman thought about blasphemy: she considered it able to bring death on the spot.
Verse 10. If we received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure the bad?

For this blessed man, struck from every side, stood all the more firmly, and though he took countless arrows, he did not give way. He emptied the devil's quiver, but he himself did not fall and was not tripped up. Like an excellent helmsman, he was not sunk when the sea raged and the waves rose, nor did he grow careless when it was calm, but he kept his skill the same in both kinds of weather. Wealth did not puff him up, nor did poverty humble him. When things flowed with the current he did not lie back at his ease, and when almost his whole household had been overturned and utter ruin had come, he was not thrown into confusion and did not let his courage be put to shame. Let the rich hear, let the poor hear. The account is useful to both, and the story profits all people, those in prosperity and those in misfortune alike. For this champion of piety, the crowned victor before the whole world, handled both kinds of weapons and set up a trophy in both. When that demon came at him with every kind of warfare, he drew up his line against them all and was proclaimed victor in all. A noble soldier knows how to fight by night, at the walls, on foot and at sea, to shoot the bow and brandish the spear, and to get the better of the enemy and prevail everywhere with slings and javelins and every manner of fighting. In the same way that noble man bore every trial with great courage: the trial of poverty, of famine, of disease, of pain, of the loss of his children, the trial that came from his friends, from his enemies, from his wife, from his servants. There was no human misfortune that was not emptied out upon his body. Yet he rose above all the nets and went higher than the devil's limed reeds. And what is still more wonderful is that everything came on him, everything to excess, and everything at once. Do not look only at the fact that he suffered so much. Add that it was not little by little, nor at intervals, but all together and at once. This is no small addition to the trials. Among all other people, first of all, no one could be found who has endured everything at once. If a man wrestles with poverty, he still enjoys health. If he is pierced by both poverty and disease, he often has the support of a wife who comforts him in his troubles and becomes a harbor for him. If he did not have such a wife, at least she did not give such ruinous advice. If she did, at least he did not lose all his children at once. If he did lose them at once, at least it was not by such a death. If it was by such a death, at least he had friends to comfort him. If he had none to comfort him, at least they did not trample on him like this. If they did trample on him, at least his servants did not reproach him too. If they reproached him, at least they did not spit in his face. If they spat in his face, at least he was not pierced by such a disease, but had a room and shelter and did not sit on the dunghill. And if he did sit on the [?] … and if he had no one to stretch out a hand to him, at least not also [?] … Verse 11. They came to him, each from his own country: Eliphaz king of the Temanites, Bildad tyrant of the Shuhites, Zophar king of the Minaeans.

Your presence is the presence of friends, and your counsel is the counsel of friends. Eliphaz means "God has scattered me," or "contempt of my God." Teman means "their failing." Zophar means "watchman," or "contempt." Bildad means "growing old," and "glorious." Shuhites means "their idle talk."
Verse 11. Now when his three friends heard of all the evils that had come upon him, they came to him, each from his own country.

If anyone asks why the friends came only after so long a time, let him consider, first, that they lived in different countries. Perhaps many people heard after a very long time, but the calamity seemed so strange as to be unbelievable: that Job should be sitting on a dunghill with no one to help him. So they waited to have the report confirmed by more witnesses, or even sent someone to see whether what was being said was true. That is how the time was spent. Besides this, once they learned the truth, since they were kings and about to go abroad, they first had to put their own household affairs in good order and set others over their subjects in their place. All these things kept them busy, and they were delayed. And unless they had been very loving and righteous men, they would not have left their own countries and kingdoms to come and visit him; they would have done their duty through others. One may also consider that the delay in their arrival was a divine dispensation. The whole contest came to an end together with the friends' debate, when God spoke and restored and crowned the righteous man. So it was by a divine dispensation that the friends were delayed, so that the illness would be prolonged, and the righteous man, having contended the longer, might be proclaimed by God with all the more justice.
Verse 11. And they came to him with one accord, to comfort him and visit him.

Symmachus rendered it this way: "For they arranged to come together to sympathize with him and console him." See from this too that still more time passed, until they had sent messages to one another and arranged to meet and arrive together.
Verse 12. And they sprinkled earth on their heads.
Verse 13. They sat beside him seven days and seven nights.

Scripture did not say that they sat by him seven days from morning to evening, nor seven nights from evening to morning. Clearly, then, they sat by him for most of the day and withdrew to see to their necessary needs. Then they came back and sat by him far into the night, and after leaving again they came to him again at dawn. This is the mark of the most genuine and sympathetic friends. Scripture, following common usage, simply said: "They sat beside him seven days and seven nights." Likewise, when it says that Jacob served fourteen years and was burned by the heat of the day and the frost of the night, did he never go under a roof? Did he get no rest the whole time? To quibble over such things is idle, for, as I said, Scripture follows common usage. But some people mock Scripture and disparage it as false even on this point: "How," they say, "could they go on without food and without sleep for so many days?" So we have been forced to follow them into this untimely pettiness.
Chapter 3

With this the second chapter is finished. As a preliminary survey of the third, we say that the righteous man does feel pain, and no one would deny it, for virtue belongs not to the insensible but to those who live wisely in the midst of their sufferings. He cannot [?] … Outwardly, he is stung most sharply by the blow to his flesh. Inwardly, as a righteous and God-loving man, he sees some people scandalized at his sufferings, as though God's glory were being disparaged because of him, if a righteous man suffers such things. For when he says, "Why have you made me your accuser?", he was not himself accusing God, God forbid! To whom could he have brought the charge? What he means is this: "Why, Master, is your name blasphemed because of me?" He is also no less troubled and dizzy with fear that he may have suffered a greater abandonment by God. Nothing punishes a God-loving soul so much as the suspicion that God has abandoned it. It would choose death ten thousand times over being counted among the living while in pain and under such a suspicion. We have heard what words of thanksgiving he uttered at the loss of his possessions and the sudden death of his children. We have heard how he corrected his wife when she thought something unfitting about the Master, what he said after the trial, the contempt and the bitter suffering, and how none of the misfortunes that befall human beings threw him into confusion. But when his friends arrived, righteous and sympathetic men, he thought it the right moment, seeing their patience and their love for him, to speak out and make known the pains of his soul. In the literal sense, what he says carries no danger. The devil had one aim: to bring the righteous man to blaspheme God. But clearly Job did nothing of the sort. Instead he spoke well of God and offered up words of thanksgiving. He curses the day of his birth and longs for death for the reasons given above. But in the deeper sense he speaks mysteries: he reflects on what has already happened and gives assurance about what is to come. Such are always the sayings of the holy prophets. Now let us turn to the words themselves and make the meaning clear, with him guiding us to the interpretation who also strengthened holy Job for his contests.
Verse 1. After this Job opened his mouth.

When a righteous man opens his mouth, one should not give casual attention to what he says, but should seek out the benefit to be drawn from his words. Such words of the saints are always full of benefit, and when a righteous man opens his mouth, he brings hidden treasures to light. That is why Paul, the chosen vessel, writes: "Our mouth is opened to you, Corinthians." And of the Lord it is written: "He opened his mouth and taught them." In general, the man who is said to open his mouth is one who has first been taught the measures of silence. So Job too opens his mouth "after this," that is, after the great trophy, after those sufferings. He does not speak rashly in his bodily agony, with his tongue running ahead of the rule of prudence; he shows his self-control in his words as well. The testimony that he opened his mouth reveals both the calm of his soul and the fittingness of his words.
Chapter 19
Verse 1. How long will you weary my soul?

Heavy loads placed on the bodies of animals make the animals that carry them tired. In the same way there are heavy words that wear out whoever hears them. Job was weighed down, as if by a heavy burden, by the force of the words spoken [?] badly and harshly, or in abuse, by the other two who had come with Bildad. Wearied in soul by what they had said, he says: "How long will you weary my soul?" And a little later: You see how he was described beforehand as "the tyrant of the Shuhites." His words are tyrannical, and when Job hears them he says: "How long will you weary my soul?" Nothing else cuts so deep into a person's soul as a harsh word. Many people have endured tortures inflicted on the body and have not been able to endure words. The perfect athlete, however, endures harsh words even when he is weary, for it is the mark of a great man to endure insult. That is why the Apostle says, among his own brave deeds: "When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become like the refuse of the world, the scum of all things, to this day." And a little later he goes on to say, about "How long will you weary my soul?": You see? This is Job, whose book is devoted above all to nothing but his courage and his endurance. Yet he feels the weariness that the harsh words of those who had come to visit him had brought on him.
Verse 3. Know only that the Lord has done this to me.

Do not think that what you see happening to me has come from anywhere but from God. So be afraid. The one who brings these things on me can bring them on you as well. Verse 3. You speak against me; you are not ashamed before me, and you press hard upon me.

People often speak against others and do wrong in doing so. But when someone has lost all shame, he says it to the other's face, not to correct him or to tell the truth, but to reproach and insult him. One must not trample on those whom God is punishing; one must lament and be afraid.
Verse 4. Yes indeed, in truth I have gone astray, and error lodges with me: I have spoken a word that I ought not to have spoken.

Then he speaks hypothetically: "I grant you" — as if implying, "Suppose it is taken for granted that I suffer these things because of my sins. Ought you then to reproach me like this?" "Error lodges with me": even if, for the sake of argument, I had done what I ought not to have done, even if I were such a man, ought you not to have been moved to respect when you saw the scourges, the oozing sores, the worms, the loss of my possessions? Instead you trample on me all the more, without pity for me or sympathy for my plight.
Verse 5. Ah, but you exalt yourselves over me and leap on me with reproach.
You do not reproach me in moderation; you leap on me. You reproach me as though you were trampling me and treading me underfoot.
Verse 6. And he has raised his fortress against me. It is as though I am shut in under the wall of my plight, a fortress I cannot escape until God decides to tear it down.
Verse 7. Behold, I laugh at reproach, and I will not speak.
This is the saying: "Overcome evil with good."
By the same author. Behold, I am minded to laugh at your reproach, not to speak.
Chapter 20
Verse 6. If his gifts go up to heaven, and his sacrifice touches the clouds,

If the gifts of the ungodly man go up to heaven, if he is exalted very high, if his sacrifice touches the clouds — when the heretic prays, when his sacrifice rises up on lofty speech, when he seems to be firmly established — then he will perish utterly. For his prayer is counted against him as sin, and his very prayer is sin.
Verse 7. For when he thinks he is already firmly established, then he will perish utterly.
This is like: "But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they are glorified and exalted, vanish like smoke and are gone."

Verse 7. And those who have seen him will say, "Where is he?" Who are those who have seen him? We of the Church, who have seen their errors, will say, "Where is he?" Verse 8. Like a dream that has flown away, he will not be found.
Such people dream and fashion phantoms. In their error they do not rest their minds on the truth, and they become like a dream that has flown away and will not be found.
Verse 10. May lesser men destroy his sons.
That is, the sons and disciples of the one who taught these things.
Verse 10. And may his hands kindle pains.
His hands, it says, that is, his deeds, will kindle punishment for him.

"And his hands": the hands of this ungodly and erring man, whose prayer is counted as sin, and whose sacrifice, if it goes up to heaven and touches the clouds, then perishes utterly. His hands will kindle pains, that is, they will live in the utmost pain. He is speaking of the sons of the lawless man.
Verse 13. The gall of an asp is in his belly.

For he has teachings that are not sweet but are the gall of an asp, that is, wicked, as with the wine of their teaching. "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom," and so on. And a little later: The gall of an asp is in the belly of the heterodox man, who is ungodly in doctrines contrary to the truth.
Verse 15. Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited up.

What other wealth is gathered unjustly than the wealth that lies in their words? It is gathered unjustly. But the Good One will not allow them, once they have fallen, to keep the wealth they gathered unjustly inside them forever; he will make them vomit it up.
Verse 15. An angel will drag him out of his house.

For an angel, through God's working and kindness, will drag him out of the house that was badly built, which is the church of evildoers. That is his house. But an angel will drag him out of his house.
Verse 17. May he not see the milking of the grazing flocks.

The heterodox man does not see the milking of the grazing flocks. The grazing flocks are souls that pasture under the Good Shepherd, who said: "I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and go out and find pasture."
Verse 18. Like strifnos, which cannot be chewed or swallowed.
Their words and doctrines are tough and dense; teachings that work against God have nothing sweet about them.

Strifnos is a plant that feels rough on the tongue of whoever chews it. So, it says, just as no one can swallow that plant, however hard he tries to grind it with his teeth, so whoever wants to enjoy what belongs to others will carry off no profit from his labors.
Verse 20. Therefore his good things will not flourish.
The things he thinks are good deeds will not flourish. When he thinks he is already full, he will be afflicted.
Verse 20. His possessions will bring him no safety.
His possessions cannot win salvation for him.
Another interpretation.
Verse 22. Every distress will come upon him, and he will send the fury of his wrath upon him.
Verse 22. Every distress will come upon him.
These words urge us to keep away from what belongs to others.
Verse 22. May he snow pains upon him. Pains instead of snow come upon such a man.
Verse 24. And he will not be saved from the hand of iron. By iron he does not mean the iron we can see and touch, but a word that cuts most sharply.
Verse 25. And may an arrow pass through his body.

These fiery arrows wound him. Verse 25. “A fire not kindled will devour him.” We learn a mystery about the punishment that is stored up, so that we may guard against suffering it. He said that a fire not kindled will devour the ungodly. The material fire we have here is not a fire that is not kindled, for it can be seen. But the fire that comes upon sinners is invisible, and it burns them within. It is a fire perceived by the mind, and it punishes. If you want an image of that fire, think of someone with a very high fever, burning up with it. You will not find the fire in him with your eyes. Yet it lies beneath and burns up his inner parts. In the same way, someone feverish with sins is burned up.
Verse 25. “And may an invader afflict his house.”
The one who made war on that people was an invader and not a proselyte. He afflicted their house, destroying what was considered the sanctuary and the city they called holy.
Verse 27. “And may heaven reveal his iniquities.”

That is, “He will suffer terrible things both from God and from heaven.” He said this because Job, after saying that he had been struck by God, also mentioned that he had been wronged by people. So he argues that everything was brought upon him because of sin.
The earth itself rises up against that people.
Verse 29. “And the possession of his goods from the overseer.”

Learn who is named “overseer” here [?]: God is called the Overseer, and bishops, the good and noble ones among them, strive in every way to bear his image. Someone who copies a royal image is honoured for copying it well, and honoured also for having adorned it. In the same way, blessed is the bishop who has understood the true Overseer, imitates him eagerly and becomes like a god among men. Or blessed is the one who has as his overseer the One who makes him truly a bishop in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 21.

Verse 5. “Look at me and be amazed.” You claim to be wise and to know why I suffer these things, since God does not sleep over people's sins. And you have dared to say that I am a sinner and have deserved to come to this.
Verse 7. “And they have grown old in wealth.” They are not newly rich. They have been rich for many years and keep increasing their wealth.

Verse 8. “Their seed is according to the soul.” The seed of the righteous is according to the spirit, for “he sows to the spirit, and from the spirit he reaps eternal life.” But “the soulish person does not receive the things of the Spirit, for they are foolishness to him.” So the seed of people like these is not according to the spirit but according to the soul, which is lower.

Verse 8. “And their children are before their eyes.” Everything they do, they do to be seen by people. For each person's works are his children. The children of the heterodox are not in the heart or in good thoughts, but before the eyes, to be seen by people.
Verse 9. “Their houses prosper.” Whenever you go into a gathering of heretics and see a crowd assembled there, take note that their houses prosper.

Verse 9. “And there is no fear anywhere.” They are fearless. They do not fear God, and they despise the Godhead. They say such things about God and are not afraid, even though it is God they are speaking about.
Verse 9. “And there is no scourge from the Lord upon them.”

By the same author. You may see someone who speaks such things against God and yet is healthy in body, can see, has his senses intact, and sometimes even seems to prosper in worldly affairs. Take note that in him, ungodly as he is, the words are fulfilled: “And there is no scourge from the Lord upon them.”

Verse 10. “Their cow did not miscarry.” By the same author. The ox is a farm animal that works together with others in farming. These people farm too. But what they farm is Sodom and Gomorrah; what they farm is Egypt. “Their cow did not miscarry.” On the contrary, it too conceived and bore offspring, so that their wicked land might be farmed.
Verse 10. “And their pregnant cow came safely through and did not slip.”
Whatever they conceive they also carry to birth, conceiving not from the fear of God but from wickedness. “Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived trouble, and brought forth lawlessness.”

Verse 11. “And they remain like everlasting sheep.” What do the words “they will remain like everlasting sheep” mean? Christ speaks of them when he says, “My sheep hear my voice, and I give them eternal life,” and so on. These are the everlasting sheep. The heterodox are imitators who want to copy the flock of Christ. They ordain for themselves bishops, presbyters, deacons and teachers, and have laity and catechumens. In imitating the everlasting sheep, they fulfil the words: “And they remain like everlasting sheep.” They are not everlasting sheep, but they remain like everlasting sheep.
Verse 11. “And their children make sport.”
Verse 12. “Taking up psaltery and lyre.”

Our people take up psaltery and lyre to sing hymns to God and glorify him. But their children, who have no understanding in themselves, take up psaltery and lyre and make sport. Whenever they take up the words of the Old Testament, they make sport of them and laugh at the oracles of the Law and the Prophets. They take up the harmonious instruments, the psaltery of the Law and the lyre of prophecy, and make sport of them.
Verse 12. “And they rejoice at the sound of a psalm.”
They too recite psalms of Valentinus and recite odes of Basilides. They utter things like these and rejoice at the sound of a psalm.
Verse 13. “And in the rest of Hades they fell asleep.”

They fell asleep in the rest not of heaven but of Hades. We, however, pray to fall asleep not in the rest of Hades but in the rest of God, in the holy heavens, with Christ reigning over us. To him be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 22.
Verse 2. “Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?”

What the Holy Spirit has arranged must be considered worthy of being written down. It is recorded so that the reader may benefit from what is read. Suppose the words of the three who came to Job were not useful, so that the reader could gain nothing from what they said to him. Then providence would not have caused the words of the three to be recorded in the book of Job as well. So it is possible to benefit from his words by looking into their teachings. Yet one should see that their words are open to blame on one point only. They blame Job, thinking that he suffers because of his sins, and they do not see that there are many other causes of what happens to people. These are the things considered good or hard, or whatever one wishes to call them. A little further on: “Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?” This teaching is sound: no human being can be a true teacher of virtue. It is written in the Psalms that the one who teaches people knowledge is none other than God. And the Prophet says, “Teach me your statutes,” because he knows that God is the true and perfect teacher. God teaches by shining on the soul of the one who learns from him and by enlightening the mind with the light, his true Word. So righteous men also teach us, once they have received the grace of teaching.
Verse 4. “And he will enter into judgment with you.”

God takes account of the one he cares for and reproves him. “And he will enter into judgment with you.” Whenever this teaching has come up in other passages, we have often said that God loves humankind so much that, even while he judges us kindly, he lets us say to him whatever we wish, as if he were standing trial alongside us. I used the words from Isaiah: “Come, let us reason together, says the Lord.” For “let us reason together” means something like this: “If you have anything to reprove me for, and my providence, as though I had neglected you or had not done what was needed, speak. And I will say whatever I have to say, and I will convince you, condemning you as deserving to be condemned.”

Verse 5. “Is not your wickedness great?” It is likely, I say, that you have not just become unjust in a simple way. You are suffering such things as none of them has ever fallen into on a scale like yours. It is likely that these things have come upon you because your offences are countless.

By the same author. He did not name sin first and then wickedness. Rather, he saw wickedness as the evil disposition, and after that he named the sins committed out of that evil disposition, which he said were countless.

Verse 5. “And your sins are countless.” Eliphaz assumes this about Job. He knew that Job was rich, and he says: “You took pledges from your brothers as though they were in debt when they were not.” This is what “you took pledges for nothing” means.
Verse 6. “You took pledges from your brothers for nothing.”

By the same author. He goes further and adds another sin of his. Is it ever possible to take clothing? Not from someone naked, but from a rich man who has many garments stored away. [?] I took clothing from the many there, yet not from the naked but from the rich. But suppose someone has only one tunic, and I strip that tunic off him on the pretext of demanding what is mine, without pitying that naked man. Then I have taken away the clothing of the naked. Many such things happen among us when we lend money and when we go after debtors. Often a debtor of ours is desperately poor and unable to repay. And we shut up our compassion and become pitiless and cruel. We do not see that he supports a wife and children and barely supports himself on the few obols he earns. We make our demands harshly, sometimes even when we have more than enough ourselves. These are the things he says in accusing Job, claiming that he took away the clothing of the naked.
Verse 7. “You did not give water to the thirsty to drink, and you deprived the hungry of a morsel.”
On the same verse. So not only doing wrong but also failing to do good makes one answerable.
All these are charges, and the things charged are truly blameworthy. But they were not true of Job, and it was not right to say them about him.

By the same author. Such things happen when debts are demanded harshly. Sometimes a person has just one morsel. Even though he does not have a whole loaf, we take it from him, saying, “But you owe it.”

Verse 9. “And you sent widows away empty.” If a widow comes into our house, let us take care never to send her away empty. Each of us should fill the widow's lap as far as we are able, in proportion to what we have.
Verse 9. “And you mistreated orphans.”

By the same author. One must harm no one, but orphans must be spared above all. For God commanded us to fight on behalf of souls that have no one to help them. More than other people, the poor, widows and orphans need help.

Verse 10. “Therefore snares have surrounded you.” By snares he means what has happened to Job. Job has fallen into these things, and his soul is caught in them as in a snare because of what has happened to him.
Verse 11. “The light has turned to darkness for you.”
You were in the light when you had your possessions, when your children were alive, when your body was healthy. But now you have gone down, as it were, into darkness, into these calamities.
On the same verse. That is, you are in desolation and under the open sky, a wanderer, an exile, homeless.
Verse 11. “And as you slept, water covered you.”

“As you slept, water covered you” means this: the opposing power covered you, because you were not watchful, because you did not sleep [?]. Scripture knows of a certain sleep of sin. That is why it gives us the command: “Give no sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, so that you may be saved like a gazelle from the noose and like a bird from the snare.”
Verse 12. “Does not the One who dwells on high watch over all?”
But you think that God, who dwells on high, does not see what is done. Yet because he watches over all things, he brings down those whose minds are puffed up by an insolent disposition.
Verse 12. “And those who are carried away by insolence he has humbled.”

If someone is carried away by insolence, and as it were dragged along by insolent habits and conduct, God humbles him. So it is likely that you too treated widows and orphans with insolence and took pledges from your brothers for nothing. That is why you have suffered these things and been humbled.
Verse 13. “And you said, What does the Mighty One know?”
It is likely that you said to yourself, “What does the Mighty One know?” As if to say, “Can God know everything?”
Verse 13. “Or will he judge through the gloom?” By the same author. But God can judge even when he is in a storm.
Verse 14. “And he goes around the circuit of heaven.”
God's providence goes around everything.
And a flood of waters will cover you.
Verse 15. “Will you not keep watch on the everlasting path?” Can you not keep watch on the everlasting path along which God's providence travels?

Verse 15. “Which righteous men have trodden.” By the same author. Righteous men have trodden the everlasting path. They walk along an everlasting path, since everything they set out to do aims at reaching the age to come. So even if they seem to walk like everyone else, their soul itself treads everlasting paths.
Verse 16. “Who were taken away before their time.”
The righteous have often died before their time. For “the righteous man, made perfect in a short time, fulfilled long years; for his soul is virtue [?] in the Lord.”
Verse 16. “Their foundations are an overflowing river.”
By the same author. The foundations of the righteous are like this. They are always advancing and always growing in good things.
Verse 18. “And he filled their houses with good things.”

By the same author. He filled the houses of the righteous with good things. I do not take these to be houses like ours. Rather, he filled their houses that are in the ruling part of the soul with good things. What good things? Self-control, justice, courage, prudence, the things that come from works. This is what it means for houses to be filled with good things.
Verse 19. “And the blameless one mocked them.”

Whom? Was it the counsel of the ungodly? For example, some people want to teach things contrary to the truth by what they say, because they hold wicked teachings. The blameless one sees this and mocks it.
Verse 20. “And fire will devour what is left of them.”
By the same author. Fire will devour whatever is left of the ungodly after the earlier ones have died.
Verse 22. “Receive a declaration from his mouth.”

I was asking myself what “declaration” means. In another edition I found “confession” in its place. So what he means is rather: “Confess your sins. Receive a declaration from the mouth of God along with confession, and take up his words from your heart.” Eliphaz said these things to admonish Job, or so he thought.
Verse 23. “But if you turn back and humble yourself before the Lord.”
He admonishes Job to turn back, because he thinks Job had sinned and had suffered these things as a result.
Verse 24. “And as beyond the torrent of Sophir.” [?] You, as it were: your speech will be richly varied and beautiful.
Verse 25. “Then the Almighty will be your helper against your enemies.”
If you submit yourself, if you confess.
Verse 25. “And he will make you pure, like silver refined by fire.”
A sound teaching, refined by fire: God [?].
Verse 26. “Then you will speak boldly before the Lord.”
By the same author. If you humble yourself and endure what has happened to you, you will speak boldly before the Lord. You will have boldness because you have put away your sins.
Verse 28. “On your ways you will be safe.”

By the same author. That is, if you keep the admonition I give you, turn back and confess. These things were said to Job, but they were not said justly, for he had not sinned. But if they are said to us, they are said justly.
Verse 28. “And he will restore to you a righteous way of life.”
To put it simply, he says: “He will restore to you a whole, lasting state that suits righteous conduct, so that your deeds will be splendid and glorious.”
Chapter 23.
Verse 2. “His hand has become heavy upon my groaning.”

He says that if the verdict on his punishments could have been given immediately, it would have been possible to find God. He says: “If only I could plead my case and meet him, and learn what he would say to me in reply to what I would say!” Do you see how he obtained what he prayed for? For this is what happened at the end of the book. “I wanted to learn what he would say to me, and whether he would go on punishing me in the same way. I said these things not because I was accusing him of injustice.”
Chapter 24.
Verse 6. “Their bread has become sweet to young men.”
He says that the ungodly find it sweet to feed young men, so that they can use them to carry out their abuses.
Chapter 27.

Verse 2. “As the Lord lives, who has judged me thus.” The devil received authority over Job and tested him night and day. He tested him first through external things, then through his very body, and after that through his friends as well. When he had tested him through his wife and Job had not been defeated, the devil brought three friends. They were not enemies and did not hold treacherous teachings. They spoke words of truth, but did not use them well or at the right time. Through these friends the devil was planning to make Job say something against Providence, to commit impiety because of his sufferings, and to lose heart because of his pains. But look at what this truly courageous and enduring man says after the speeches of the three. Eliphaz had completed three discourses and Zophar two. When these were finished and they had fallen silent, look at what he answers, after what he said in the proem, as Scripture calls it. Let us pay attention to the text and see what he answers.
Verse 1. “And Job continued and said in his proem:”
Verse 2. “As the Lord lives, who has judged me thus, and the Almighty, who has embittered my soul,” and so on.

I know what has moved you to provoke me. But I swear to you, and I swear by the living Lord himself. He is the one who judged that I should suffer these things and handed me over to these calamities. He is the one who gave authority for me to be tested with such trials and tormented. I swear by the Lord and I say: As the Lord lives, who has judged me thus, and the Almighty, who has embittered my soul.
Verse 5. “Far be it from me to declare you righteous until I die.”
If I were to agree with what you say, namely that you have understood why I have suffered these things, I would be declaring you righteous until I die.
Verse 5. “For I will not part with my innocence.”
I will not stop paying heed to righteousness. I will always remember to hold fast to it.
Verse 6. “For I am not aware of having done anything wrong.”
He has great boldness about his former life and also about how he behaved during his calamity. So he says: “I am not aware of having done anything wrong.”
Chapter 28.
Verse 12. “And where is the place of knowledge?” Knowledge is grasping, through contemplation, the things that do not change. Understanding is discernment.
Verse 15. “And silver will not be weighed out in exchange for it.”
Nothing is worth as much as wisdom. Even if you take the silver and the gold in a simpler sense, Job will at once be saying that nothing is worthy of wisdom.
Verse 16. “With precious onyx and sapphire.”
Wisdom will not be compared even with precious onyx, nor will it be matched with sapphire.
Verse 18. “Lofty things and gabis will not be mentioned.”

Neither lofty things nor gabis are worthy of wisdom. The word seems to be used of [?], something like grape-stones [?]. Some say that gabis is the name for what is heaped up above the rim of a medimnus measure, which is called the cumulatum.
Verse 18. “And draw out wisdom above the innermost things.”

The innermost things are those around India, or in the country beyond it, where precious stones are found. That country brings people these things, which the rich consider marvellous. So draw wisdom to yourself beyond those innermost things. Or, “above the innermost things” may mean above the utterly unspeakable holy mysteries of God within. Draw out wisdom above all things, many as they are.
Verse 21. “It has escaped the notice of every human being.” It has escaped the notice of every human being, even if he is a prophet, even if he is an apostle.
Chapter 29.

Verse 6. “When my ways flowed with butter.” We said earlier that the ways Job travelled were virtues. So his ways flowed with butter. He travelled the road of self-control, and his self-control was poured out, as it were. As a result many people, even infants, were nourished by Job's self-control, by Job's righteousness and by his courage. This is what “When my ways flowed with butter” means.
Verse 6. “And my mountains flowed with milk.”
Job's mountains were all his lofty and great thoughts, and he climbed them.
Verse 7. “When I went out at daybreak into the city.”
He devoted himself to teaching and to helping others. He spoke not out of self-love but out of a love that seeks the common good.
Verse 9. “Laying a finger on their mouth.”

“Laying a finger on their mouth” will seem to be a sign of silence. But since, as we have often shown, the hand stands for works, it may show that they laid their work upon their mouth. With what little they had done, they realised that they were not worthy to speak in the presence of Job, whose works were greater.

Verse 10. “And those who heard me called me blessed.” By the same author. Before his torments began, Job was so great that those who heard him called him blessed. They marvelled at how he understood and grasped such great things and was able to benefit those who heard him.
Verse 10. “For their tongue stuck to their throat.”
Those who heard me and called me blessed for what I said had their tongues stick to their throats.

Verse 11. “For the ear heard and called me blessed.” By the same author. It is written of Moses that he was afraid to look at God because of the overwhelming greatness of his splendour. In the same way, you might understand that Job's progress in wisdom was overwhelming. Those who heard him could not look into the brilliance of his thoughts, and because they could not, they turned their eyes away, unable to follow the depth of his mind. That is why he says:
Verse 11. “And the eye that saw me turned away.”
Aquila and Symmachus translated it as “bore witness about me.” Others have “And the eye that saw turned away,” in the sense of “I am not able to contradict him.”
Verse 12. “For I rescued the poor from the hand of the powerful.”

Let us look at his brave deeds and lay them out. This has meaning according to the letter, and it has far more interpretation according to the higher sense. According to the letter, we ought, as far as we are able, to help the poor who are oppressed by the powerful.
Verse 15. And a foot to the lame.
He himself gave steps, the feet of the soul, to those who were lame; and by his word he himself became their foot.
(20) Verse 16. And the case I did not know, I searched out. He teaches us how we must judge if we are ever called to arbitrate between brothers, so as to settle their affairs.
Chapter 32.
Verse 1. And Job ceased from his words. And his three friends also kept quiet and no longer answered Job, for Job was righteous before them.

He did not simply cease. His heart, which understood divine things, did not cease. For there is a time for every matter under heaven, a time to keep silence and a time to speak. So when it was time to answer the three, he spoke; when the time came, after he had silenced them, he fell silent. And I think the words "Job ceased" are said in his praise.
Verse 7. Therefore I kept quiet, afraid to declare my own knowledge to you (21).

He has knowledge of how people suffer; of why some people fall into adversities when one looks at this life alone; of how many who are unjust prosper. I saw people doing wrong and breaking the law, and my feet almost slipped. If I look at this life alone, my steps nearly gave way.
Verse 10. It is not the long-lived who are wise.
(22) For it does not follow, he says, that only the old are wise; one can also hear something noble from youth. For if time makes people wise, much more does God.
Verse 18. For the spirit of my belly is destroying me.

(23) Just as a woman becomes pregnant, and when the child being born in her (24) has been formed, she goes into labour until she brings forth what she had earlier conceived, so understand that something like this (25) happens also in the soul of one who loves learning. For it conceives the word, and as it is being declared, it forms it and shapes it in due order. And when, after shaping and forming it, the word has become ready, the soul does not hand it over like an unready and imperfect miscarriage, but, I would say, as something brought to term and perfected.
(26) Verse 19. And my belly is like a wineskin of new wine fermenting, tied shut.
It seems to me that the saying in the Gospel comes from this: No one puts new wine into old wineskins.
Verse 20. I will speak, so that I may find rest, once I have opened my lips.
(27) Someone who has found an intelligent listener, and is full of words, finds rest in speaking, and says: I will speak, so that I may find rest.
Verse 22. For I do not know how to show partiality.
For I do not know how to show partiality. I do not have this skill, to defer to persons; rather, I disregard people, and the shame one feels before mortals, and the respect one shows them.
Verse 22. Otherwise moths will eat me too.
As though moths devour those who show partiality to people.
Chapter 35.
Verse 6. If you have sinned, what will you do?

If you look up to heaven and consider the clouds, you will understand what you have sinned. What must you do? Go to the high priest and entreat him to offer a sacrifice for you. For if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
Verse 6. And if you have committed many lawless deeds, what can you do?

(28) You will do this great thing: you will undo your many lawless deeds. That is why, for the incurable ills which we cannot heal ourselves, Jesus Christ came from heaven, to heal what was incurable, so that this might come true: Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered (29).
Verse 7. Since, then, you are righteous, what will you give him?
But if you are righteous before God, what do you have to give on the strength of your righteousness?
(30) And if you are righteous, as you say, what will you add to him?
Verse 10. He who appoints watches in the night.
(31) He recounts the praises of God, his commendations and hymns. He who appoints the night watches is God himself.

(32) I want to see how God is the one who appoints the night watches. This whole age is night; it is darkness. The light is being kept for you. The light you see now, you see in a mirror. And: In your light we shall see light. One day we shall see it. So the whole age is night; and since it is night, there are many wars (33), and many wild beasts prowl about.
Verse 11. He who separates me from the four-footed beasts of the earth.

(34) If you are a sinner, you have not been separated from the four-footed beasts of the earth. For man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless cattle and became like them. If you are a sinner, you have not been separated from the four-footed beasts of the earth; rather, it is said to you: Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding. — And a little further on: If you are a sinner, if you are a fornicator, if you are lustful, you will not be separated from the four-footed beasts. They became stallions mad for mares. That is why he says with confidence that he was set apart: He who separates me from the four-footed beasts of the earth.
Chapter 40.
Verse 3. No, but gird up your loins like a man. I give you freedom to speak. I will question you, and you answer me.

(35) God is already giving him a prize. He questions a man: he inquires of him and grants him the right to answer. Had Job not been victorious, he would not have received this; had he not endured, he would not have heard: Gird up your loins like a man. I will question you, and you answer me.

By the same. Let no one answer God until he has become a man and girds up his loins like a man. For as long as his loins are not girded but loose, not bound round or drawn tight, he cannot fittingly answer the Lord.
Verse 3. I will question you, and you answer me.

The full rewards of the contests are laid up, after this life, for those who have competed well. Nonetheless, even now the grace of God gives the athletes a pledge. That is why, when Job had fought the greatest contests—when, having lost his possessions, he glorified the one who had given them; when, bereft of his children, he gave thanks to the one who had taken them; when, seeing worms coming up out of his body, he was not overcome by his sufferings—God gives him a foretaste and pledge of the prizes, speaking to him through whirlwind and clouds. So, having heard the earlier words, when he ought to answer God, he is silent, as though he had no freedom to answer him. For he did not yet know what was later written by Moses, that Moses spoke and God answered him with a voice. Not knowing this, then, he is unwilling to answer God. But God gives him freedom to speak. And after other things: So great is God's kindness that he takes on the role not of one who judges, but of one who is judged together with man. And many Scriptures have taught this. Come, let us reason together, says the Lord. And: My people—or rather, God will plead with his people—My people, what have I done to you, or how have I troubled you? Answer me; and so on.
Verse 3. Do not reject my judgment.

(36) Do not reject this judgment of mine. Let us remember this saying as a useful one. Whenever God judges that we should suffer something—lose a child, lose a ruler, fall ill in body, endure any of these things whatever—we cannot suffer any of them unless God has judged it. For not even a sparrow falls into a snare without the will of the Father who is in heaven. Since, then, none of these things happens without God's judgment, it is said to the one who suffers:
Do not reject my judgment; do not deny (37) that I have passed judgment concerning you.
Verse 3. Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?

I am explaining myself to you. You were righteous, but it was not evident. You had endurance; I had to give your endurance an occasion to shine. You had courage, but it was hidden within you; the sufferings that befell you displayed your courage. And a little further on: Let us remember these words in times of adversity, and let us imagine that we hear God present and saying to us: Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous? Let us not be shown to be unrighteous or ungodly.
Verse 5. Take up, then, loftiness and power.
Crown yourself, clothe yourself with glory, clothe yourself with honour.
Verse 6. Send out angels in wrath, and humble every insolent one.
Verse 7. Quench the arrogant.

The insolent one made war on you. The insolent one once said to me: Stretch out your hand; he said to me: Touch all that he has; he said to me about you that you would surely bless me to my face. Yet you have conquered. That is why I say to you: Take courage; humble every insolent one, and humble his angels. That one became arrogant against you; but you, quench the arrogant. That one was ungodly against you; but you, strike down the ungodly at once.
Verse 8. And fill their faces with dishonour.
Convict sinners by showing them to be sinners. Fill their faces with dishonour through the reproof that is in you.
Verse 10. But see, there are beasts with you; it eats grass like oxen.

The beasts are the opposing powers, about which the Prophet prayed, saying: Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you. The beasts are the opposing powers, over which you, O man, have received authority. If you serve God, you will tread on the asp and the basilisk.
Verse 10. But see, there are beasts with you.
By the same. With you, Job; with everyone who endures; with everyone who has conquered.
Verse 10. It eats grass like oxen.
He means the worms, which came out of him and were devouring him. For he says: [?] my hand by you; and see, it devours as if grass (38).
Verse 11. And its power is at the navel of its belly.
(39) This is the first power ranged against a man. It is from here that it begins to make him a fornicator.

By the same. This is to indicate the female, to show that it wages war not only against those who have seed. Very fittingly he spoke of the loins in the case of the male, and the navel of the belly in the case of the woman: See, its strength is in its loins, and its power is at the navel of its belly.
Verse 25. And the nations of the Phoenicians divide it up among them.

(40) Since the Canaanites, who are also the Phoenicians, are reproached for great wickedness, he therefore says: The nations of the Phoenicians will divide him up. Each one takes some part of the dragon, if he is a Canaanite and Phoenician by race.
Verse 26. And all that floats, gathered together, could not carry a single hide of its tail.

(41) All floating things together cannot kill the last and furthest parts of the dragon. Human beings, using their bodies as ships, cannot carry a single hide of his tail. By themselves they cannot; but when divine power watches over us, we can carry off not just a single hide of his tail but the whole of him, and kill the whole of him. And each of us, as far as it lies with him, puts the devil to death, as the Apostle says: And God will soon crush Satan under your feet.
Chapter 41.
Verse 4. Who will uncover the face of his garment?

Why did he not say, "Who will uncover his face?" What is the garment doing here? For who, he says, will uncover the face of his garment? To understand what is said, let us use the example of masks that people put on, which do not show what the wearers are, but what they want to seem to be. Actors on the stage, for instance, put on masks, sometimes of generals, sometimes of other kings, sometimes of women. Their own face is hidden, and what they are does not appear; what is seen is what they seem to be. Such is the dragon. He never shows his own face; but if (42) he takes on a face to deceive people, he uses that (43). And indeed this enemy has many masks, and for each vice he puts on the face of a virtue. And a little further on, on what follows.
The rest of the verse quoted above.

(44) Who is able to expose the face he has put on? Who is able to uncover and show [?] (45) what the dragon is within? Such too are certain others, his disciples, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.
Verse 4. And who could enter into the fold of his breastplate?

Do you see? This is called a breastplate—both chest and breastplate—where the ruling faculty is. His breastplate is not simple. Nothing about him is simple. He is deceitful; he is folded over. So who could enter into the fold of his breastplate? A saint, however, can expose him and show that his breastplate is folded; but the saint's is not folded.

Verse 5. Who will open the gates of his face? He hides what is stored up within. Who, then, will open the gates of his face? Who is there able to expose and show how much deceit, how much venom, how many evils he has stored up?
Verse 5. Around his teeth is fear.

Of these it is said: You have broken the teeth of sinners. And: The Lord will break the jaw-teeth of the lions. This fear is not the fear of God, but the fear that is around his teeth. But if you have Christ within you, do not be troubled by this fear. For you shall fear the Lord your God, and apart from him fear no other.
Verse 6. His innards are bronze shields.
That is, his hidden doctrines and thoughts. It is all asps' venom, everything within him. And these asps are not soft but hard; for they are hard shields.
Verse 10. Out of his mouth.
The blasphemies and words of ungodly and godless teachers.
Verse 10. Out of his mouth go burning torches, and braziers of fire are flung out.

(46) I think that all ungodly introducers of godless doctrines are, properly speaking, members of the dragon; and if you want to hear the names of the dragon's members, who are they? The dragon's mouth might also be understood figuratively, and accordingly as the source of the words that destroy. For out of his mouth come [?] torches of fire; out of his mouth come [?] braziers of fire. If ever I have heard an accusing discourse that, on the pretext of Christianity, accuses the Creator—one, for instance, advocating the teachings of Marcion, of Valentinus, and of Basilides—when they speak ill of the Maker of heaven and earth, when they say that he is not [?], nor of spiritual substance, the sort of things these people say, you will see that out of the mouths of such people go burning torches, and braziers of fire are flung out. Therefore, knowing this, let us guard ourselves, so that those torches may never burn us, and the braziers of fire may never touch us.
Verse 13. And power lodges in his neck.

There is an evil power. But the weakness that my Saviour and Lord took on for my sake, which is called the weakness of God, has conquered his power. For the weakness of God, the Apostle says, is stronger than men; and I would say it is stronger than the power of the dragon.
Verse 14. And the flesh of his body is glued together.
He could have said: And the flesh of his body is united.

But he did not say it, for it is not united; that is not so. What is one in him is many; or rather, things that seem to be one are glued together, as shown by the speaker saying "glued together," not "united."
Verse 15. His heart is set hard as a stone, and it stands like an anvil that cannot be hammered out.

Not hammered out, not yielding to reason, but [?] (47) hard, impossible to hammer out, unyielding. And if anyone has drawn power from the devil, this dragon, he has a heart that cannot be hammered out and does not yield to the hammer. But if anyone is gold, following the word of the goldsmith (48), he yields until he becomes a sheet of gold and receives the impressions of God's letters, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
Chapter 42.
Verse 10. And the Lord gave Job double all that he had before, twice over.

(49) The noble athlete, who endured every trial, the most courageous Job, receives the prizes of his endurance, as Scripture says: Everything double compared with before. But the Lord Jesus Christ gives prizes not twofold but a hundredfold. For he says: Whoever leaves father or mother, house, brothers, sisters for my sake or for the sake of the gospel—as is written in Mark—will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life. Job would not have received double what he had before had he not displayed double virtue.
